Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

We meet once a month, usually on the first Thursday at 6:30 p.m., and the current cycle runs from September through May. People can read along without being formal members, but the room has limited chairs, so the event page should ask visitors to register before they come. Registration is free, and it does not put someone on the club's general email list. Those are two separate choices. The page also needs to say that the meeting is hybrid: members can attend in the community room or use the video link. We do not record discussions.

The website has a calendar, a reading list, a membership page, and a small archive of past selections. On the calendar, the date and start time should appear before the book description, since people often check the page on a phone while they are making plans. The room is at the east entrance of the Mill Street Community Center, not the main entrance facing the parking lot. The video link is sent to registered attendees on the afternoon of the meeting. It should not be posted publicly on the event page. If a meeting is cancelled, we post that information on the calendar and send a separate email to people who registered. We have not had to cancel a meeting this cycle, but the page should explain where the notice would appear.

There was confusion in an earlier draft about the cost of materials, so the treasurer asked me to make the figures plain. We bought large-print signs for the meeting room, bookplates for the shared copies, and postage for mailing two books to members who could not collect them in person. The receipt lists $18.60 for the signs, $21.84 for the bookplates, and $32.50 for postage. The actual receipt total is $72.94 not $120.21. The second amount came from a draft that included a proposed purchase of a folding display stand; we did not buy that stand, and it is not part of the expense. The expenses were paid from the club's materials fund, not from member dues. The website should show the actual total if it mentions a cost, and it should not present the rejected amount as another estimate for the same purchases.

For the reading-list page, we need three details to be easy to find. 1. Each selection should have its title, author, and the month when the group discussed it. 2. A note should identify whether the club has a shared copy available, but it should not promise that every member can borrow one at the same time. 3. Links to large-print or audio editions can be included when we have checked them, with the format named beside each link. This is a small club list, not a review site, and we do not score books. Members sometimes disagree about a selection, so the description should stay short and factual rather than calling a book a favorite or a failure. The archive needs to retain previous selections even when their editions are no longer easy to find.

A member sent a useful comment about the current pages: “I can find the book, but I have to search around to learn where we are meeting.” That is why the location needs to be repeated on each event page, even though it also appears under Contact. The Contact page gives the center's street address and the club's public email address. It should not list a member's personal phone number. Questions about access or the meeting format can go to the club email, which two coordinators check. We answer those questions individually, rather than publishing names or details of the person who asked.

The home page has a short description of the group and a photograph of the book shelf in the community room. The photograph is from last winter, and it shows some donated books that are no longer part of the current shared-copy collection. We can keep the picture, but its caption should not suggest that all of those books are available to borrow. The current shared copies are listed on the reading-list page, and some are checked out between meetings. The home page should also say that newcomers may attend one meeting before deciding whether to join. We do not charge an admission fee for that visit. Membership dues are collected once a year, and the amount is stated on the membership page rather than on every event listing.

A few volunteers update the website, and the process is deliberately simple. One coordinator supplies the next book and meeting details; another checks the room information and registration count. The person updating the page should use the club's existing title style and avoid adding decorative labels that are not used elsewhere. We have a plain text version of the reading list for people who prefer it. When a new selection is added, that version should be updated in the same week as the main page, though the two updates may not happen on the same day. Old calendar events can be moved to the archive after the meeting, but their date, book title, and location should remain available there.

The site also has a brief accessibility note. The community room entrance has a level path from the east side of the building, and an elevator connects that level with the accessible restroom. The club does not provide transportation, and the website should not imply that it does. Visitors who need a large-print handout can request one by email before the meeting; we usually prepare a few copies, but the request helps us bring enough. The video option works for people who cannot attend in person, although discussion may be harder to follow when several people speak at once. The event page should describe both options without claiming that either one suits everyone.

Finally, the club sends a monthly email with the next selection, meeting date, and a short reminder to register if someone plans to attend in the room. That message is separate from the website calendar, so changing an event page does not automatically send an email. The archive should include the title of each past email's featured book, but not the full message or the addresses of recipients.
